title: Why Escrows Get Delayed (and How Agents Can Prevent It)
description: Most escrow delays trace back to a handful of predictable causes. Here's what slows loans down and how agents and loan officers can keep closings on schedule.
image_alt: Two men sitting at a table with papers and a pen

faq.a: Slow borrower documents, appraisal timing or value issues, title problems, insurance delays, and last-minute changes to the buyer's finances are the most common causes.

faq.q: How can agents help keep a loan on track?
faq.a: Set expectations with buyers about document turnaround, share key contract dates with the loan officer immediately, and check in on loan status before every contingency deadline.

faq.q: When is the Closing Disclosure sent?
faq.a: The borrower must receive the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing, so last-minute changes can push the closing date.

body_html:
Every agent has lived through it: everything looks fine, then a week before closing the lender needs "just one more thing," the seller is packed, and the buyer's lease is ending. Delays happen, but most aren't random. They come from a short list of causes that can be spotted early.

The usual suspects

CauseEarly warning signPrevention
Borrower documentsSlow responses in the first weekSet expectations at contract; same-day turnaround
AppraisalAggressive price or few compsOrder immediately; prepare comps for the appraiser
Title issuesLiens, trusts, estates, or recent transfersOpen title fast and review the prelim right away
Homeowners insuranceWildfire areas or older roofsShop insurance in week one
Changes to buyer financesNew job, new car, big depositsRemind buyers what not to do
Condo reviewHOA management slow to respondOrder the questionnaire on day one

The first 72 hours set the pace

Most of what goes wrong late in escrow could have been caught in the first three days. Here's what I like to see happen right after acceptance:

  1. The fully executed contract goes to the loan officer the same day
  2. Escrow and title are opened and the preliminary title report is requested
  3. The appraisal is ordered
  4. For condos, the HOA questionnaire is ordered
  5. The buyer starts shopping homeowners insurance
  6. Everyone has the contingency removal dates on their calendar

Help your buyers help themselves

Buyers don't cause delays on purpose. They just don't know how sensitive underwriting is. Sharing a simple list, like my post on nine things not to do during escrow, sets expectations in a way that doesn't sound like a lecture coming from you.

Know the three-day rule

Federal rules require the borrower to receive the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing. Certain changes after that, such as a significant change in the loan's cost or the loan product, can restart the waiting period. Practically, that means final numbers need to be settled earlier than many people expect. Changes to credits or repairs in the final days can create a timing problem.

Communication that actually works

  • One weekly status update from the loan officer to both agents, even when nothing's changed
  • A call before each contingency deadline, not just an email
  • Immediate notice of any issue, with a proposed fix and a new date if needed

Listing agents appreciate this more than anything. Proactive communication is one of the main reasons sellers accept one buyer's offer over another's when terms are close.

Handling a delay when it happens

Even with the best preparation, some escrows slip. When it happens, how the team responds matters as much as the cause. A good response includes:

  1. Immediate notice to both agents, with the reason and a realistic new timeline
  2. A written extension of any contingency or closing dates, signed before deadlines pass
  3. A check on the rate lock and whether an extension is needed
  4. A plan for the seller and buyer, including move-out and move-in logistics, rent-backs, or storage

Delays handled this way rarely damage relationships. Delays discovered on closing day almost always do.

Insurance has become a bigger factor

In parts of California, homeowners insurance has become harder and slower to place, particularly in areas with wildfire exposure. Lenders require proof of coverage before funding, so insurance can turn into a closing-day bottleneck if it's left too late. Encourage buyers to request quotes during the first week of escrow, or even before writing an offer on higher-risk properties.

The takeaway

On-time closings aren't luck. They come from a fast start, buyers who know the rules, and a loan officer who communicates before problems become emergencies. Build those habits into every transaction and delays become the exception.
